'''Rumford's Soup''' ('''''Rumfordsche Suppe''''', also called '''economy soup''')<ref name="Hagemann"/><ref name="Walker"/> was an early effort in scientific [[nutrition]]. It was invented by [[Benjamin Thompson]], [[Reichsgraf]] von Rumford, circa 1800 and consumed in [[Munich]] and greater [[Bavaria]],<ref name="Walker"/> where he was employed as an advisor to [[Charles Theodore, Elector of Bavaria]]. It was used as a ration for the poor,<ref name="Kellogg Baynes Smith"/><ref name="Report"/> for Bavarian workhouses<ref name="Luxemburg"/> and military workhouses,<ref name="Dallas"/> and prisoners. Count Rumford has been credited in many instances for "establishing the first real [[soup kitchen]]."<ref name="Bramen">{{cite web | last=Bramen | first=Lisa | title=Count Rumford and the History of the Soup Kitchen | website=Smithsonian | date=December 29, 2010 | url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/count-rumford-and-the-history-of-the-soup-kitchen-26785526/ | access-date=January 24, 2015}}</ref>

As a reformatory measure, the Bavarian government intended to institute workhouses  for those on [[Welfare (financial aid)|welfare]]. Rumford's charge was to provide the cheapest possible ration that was still a high-calorie, nutritious food. The soup came to be well known among philanthropic-minded people throughout Germany at the time, and Rumford set up his soup kitchens in many German cities.<ref name="Wilde">{{cite book | last=Wilde | first=O. | title=The Woman's World | publisher=Source Book Press | issue=v. 1-3 | year=1990 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JFcCAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA280 | access-date=January 24, 2015 | page=280| isbn=9780876810781 }} ISSN 0043-7425</ref>

Rumford's soup was a common base for inexpensive military rations in Central Europe for much of the nineteenth and twentieth century.<ref name="Luxemburg"/>
